figureObjective: Compare specular and diffuse reflection for the same parallel incident rays while preserving the local law of reflection.

claims.text: At each point of incidence, theta_r equals theta_i when both angles are measured from the local normal.
A smooth surface with aligned local normals preserves an ordered reflected direction.
A rough surface has varying local orientations, so parallel incident rays leave in many global directions.
Diffuse reflection changes the distribution of global directions but does not suspend the local law of reflection.

anchors.location: OpenStax Physics 16.1, paragraph fs-id1167067294202 and Figure 16.3; official PDF pages 496-497
anchors.normalizedEquation: theta_r = theta_i, with both angles measured from the local normal at the point of incidence

anchors.location: OpenStax Physics 16.1, paragraph fs-id1167067150525; official PDF page 497
anchors.exactQuote: Because the light is reflected from different parts of the surface at different angles, the rays go in many different directions, so the reflected light is diffused.

anchors.location: OpenStax Physics 16.1, Figure 16.4 caption; official PDF page 497
anchors.exactQuote: Here, many parallel rays are incident, but they are reflected at many different angles because the surface is rough.

elements.meaning: The same ordered incident-ray set used in both panels.
Surface whose local normals remain aligned across the shown region.
Surface whose local orientations and normals vary across incidence points.
Normal at one point of incidence used to measure theta_i and theta_r.
Reflected rays leaving a rough surface in many global directions.

allowedVariation.rule: Panels may be horizontal or vertical if the same incident-ray set is visibly reused.
Surface and ray colors may vary; local normals must remain distinguishable from physical rays.
Mirror or page icons may label everyday cases but may not replace the local-normal construction.

mutations.description: Measure an angle from the surface or show theta_r unequal to theta_i at a local incidence point.
Claim that rough surfaces violate the local law of reflection.
Make normals look like physical rays or omit normals while displaying angle arcs.
Draw distributed rays from a single flat local orientation, hiding the rough-surface basis.
